You are shown a snapshot of US macroeconomic and market data as it was known at the end of one month between 2007 and 2026.

Estimate which month the snapshot describes. Use only the figures supplied plus your general knowledge of economic history.

Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"year": yyyy, "month": m, "confidence": c, "cues": ["...", "..."]}
Rules: year is an integer from 2007 to 2026; month is an integer from 1 to 12; c in [0, 1] is your confidence that the guess is within 6 months of the truth; 1 to 3 short cues citing the inputs.
text:
The pattern is low core CPI relative to the past 3 years, a low 10-year yield, a policy rate somewhat below its 3-year average but rising over 12 months, and an unemployment rate above its 3-year average but falling. Industrial production is strong.

One candidate is late 2017 to 2019. A 36-month window ending in 2019 would include the 2016 lows, which doesn't fit. The 10-year yield z of -2 with a 3-month change of -1 suggests yields fell sharply. The policy rate z of -0.5 with a 12-month change of +1.5 suggests hikes over the past year, yet the rate is still below its 3-year average.

That is odd, since a hiking cycle would normally put the rate above its 3-year mean. It could fit mid-2024 to early 2025 only if the rate were high, and it isn't.

Another candidate is 2010-2011. Core CPI at -2 fits a period of low core inflation. The policy rate there would be near zero, though, so it would show no 12-month change.

A better fit is 2026, or perhaps late 2025. The 36-month window would run from 2022-2025. Core CPI would be low versus the 2023 highs, which fits. The policy rate would be below its average, since cuts began in September 2024 and the rate was about 3.6-3.9% against an average near 4.5. But the 12-month change of +1.5 doesn't fit cuts.

Another option is 2019, with a window from 2016 to 2019. The rate was rising through 2018, but headline CPI there wouldn't be this low.

Consider 2017-18 instead. The unemployment rate z of +1 with a 12-month change of -1 suggests it is falling from a high level, which points to a recovery. The window would be 2008-2011 at the earliest, but then the policy rate would be well below average.

What about mid-2019? The window is mid-2016 to mid-2019. The policy rate is now above its average, so that fails.

Try late 2023 to 2024 instead. Unemployment would be low, so that doesn't fit.

Try 2020-21. In mid-2021 the window runs from mid-2018 to mid-2021, and unemployment is high but falling. Industrial production is rising 12m. The policy rate would be below average (z -0.5 is plausible), but its 12-month change would be about 0, not +1.5. The 10-year yield z of -2 doesn't fit that period either.

Try 2012 instead. The window runs 2009-2012, and the rate is near zero.

Try late 2010. Unemployment would be falling, but IP z +1.5 is plausible. Core CPI would be at record lows, which fits. The 10-year yield would be falling, which fits. But the policy rate would show no 12-month change, which doesn't fit.

I'll go with mid-2019 as a rough guess: the 10-year yield fell sharply into August 2019, treasuries were strong, and equities were weak in the month. The equity-bond correlation is negative, which fits 2019. Gold was +0.5 on the month.
